decision: Which approach best resolves: Choose the write-concurrency strategy for SQLite in a Digital Sales Room where a Python backend serves the UI and must log every write to an audit table.

state.problem: Choose the write-concurrency strategy for SQLite in a Digital Sales Room where a Python backend serves the UI and must log every write to an audit table.

candidate_solutions.single_writer_wal: One long-lived backend process is the ONLY writer to the shared SQLite file, in WAL mode with a generous busy_timeout. Sub-agents never write the shared database: they write source code and pytest tests that run against a throwaway temp database per test. The audit log is written by the backend in the same transaction as the data change, so audit rows can never be lost or reordered relative to the change they describe.
candidate_solutions.shared_db_direct_writes: Sub-agents and tests may write the shared SQLite file directly, in WAL mode with busy_timeout and retry-on-busy. Maximally convenient for ad-hoc inspection, but audit rows can be written by a process other than the one that changed the data, and an abandoned test can leave the shared file locked or dirty.
candidate_solutions.per_writer_databases: Each git worktree gets its own SQLite file and audit logs are merged afterwards. Zero cross-process contention, but merging is lossy on ordering, audit ids can collide across worktrees, and the running UI cannot show a coherent audit trail.

context.requirement_1: Every SQLite change must be recorded in an audit table the UI displays.
context.requirement_2: 100+ sub-agents work in isolated git worktrees, then their branches merge.
context.requirement_3: The app must be runnable and verifiable on localhost.
context.conclusion_already_established: Sub-agents write CODE, not rows in the shared database. Their tests use per-test temporary databases. Therefore the only production writer is the backend process, and the real concurrency question is just multiple backend workers plus test runs.

state.problem: WF-017 white-label rooms on a custom domain: the vendor's own docs say that re-pointing a custom domain breaks every previously shared link ('all shared links would need to be reshared otherwise the links will appear broken'), while default-host links keep working. What should our product do when a customer changes their custom domain after rooms have been shared?

candidate_solutions.alias_history: Keep every domain the customer has ever verified as a permanent alias that still resolves rooms. Nothing shared ever breaks. Costs: aliases accumulate, must be surfaced and individually removable, and the customer cannot fully retire a domain they gave up.
candidate_solutions.windowed_grace: Serve the retired domain for a bounded grace period (e.g. 30 days), then it stops resolving. Balances link stability against unbounded alias accumulation. Costs: a time-based behaviour that is hard to reason about and can still surprise a buyer on day 31.
candidate_solutions.break_on_change: Mirror the vendor exactly: changing the custom domain immediately invalidates old-host room URLs, and the API returns an explicit list of affected share links so they can be reshared. Simplest model. Costs: breaks the white-label promise the moment a customer fixes a typo in their domain, which is the most common real cause of a change.

decision: Which approach best resolves: What is the correct IDENTITY of a shared room link in WF-017, given that the customer may re-point their custom domain after rooms have been shared?

state.problem: What is the correct IDENTITY of a shared room link in WF-017, given that the customer may re-point their custom domain after rooms have been shared?

candidate_solutions.secret_is_identity: Make the non-removable per-room link secret the identity, and treat the host as pure presentation. Resolution looks up the secret regardless of which verified host the request arrived on, so the default host and every previously-verified custom domain keep resolving the same room. Re-pointing the domain therefore rewrites the address without breaking a single link. Inspired directly by Liferay's split between Friendly URL (readable address) and External Reference Code (stable integration key), and by Qwilr's non-removable secret.
candidate_solutions.alias_history: Keep every domain the customer has ever verified as a permanent alias row that resolves rooms. Nothing shared ever breaks, but aliases accumulate, must be listed and individually removable, and the host is still part of resolution.
candidate_solutions.windowed_grace: Serve a retired domain for a bounded grace period (e.g. 30 days), then stop resolving it. Time-based behaviour, easy to surprise a buyer on day 31.
candidate_solutions.break_on_change: Mirror the vendor exactly: changing the custom domain immediately invalidates old-host room URLs, and the API returns the list of affected share links so they can be reshared.

context.extra_evidence_1: Qwilr keeps old links working: 'If you have previously shared any Qwilr Pages using our standard domain pages.qwilr.com, those links will continue working after your custom domain takes effect.' So the vendor already treats hosts as coexisting aliases, not exclusive.
context.extra_evidence_2: Liferay explicitly separates the two concerns: 'Friendly URL - Determines the URL for this room. Changing it changes the room's address, so update any links that point to the old one.' versus 'External Reference Code - the key other systems use to find this room.'
context.extra_evidence_3: Qwilr's link secret is non-removable and host-independent: 'Qwilr automatically appends a unique, non-removable identifier (link secret) to the end of every page URL for security purposes ... This applies even after a custom domain is configured.' It is a capability token for one page, not an address.
context.product_promise: open-source Digital Sales Room, every write audited, schema-flexible JSON records
context.constraint: Room identity must remain a stable integration key so other systems keep resolving rooms (Liferay's External Reference Code requirement).

Our storage envelope has no account concept - only the fixed vocabulary id, collection, room_id, revision, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at - and rooms are the primary buyer-facing entity. candidate_solutions.room_scoped_with_account_facade: Store the custom domain as an ordinary room record's field (e.g. data.domain), so it is room scoped and needs no new envelope vocabulary or migration. Grouping by a shared value in the data JSON can be done later with the existing dynamic index (find on data.domain), so account rollup is possible without redesign. Room-level matches the product's existing mental model.
candidate_solutions.domain_record_with_room_refs: Introduce a separate 'domain' collection whose records hold the verified domain and reference rooms by room_id, making an account-level fan-out explicit and queryable. Cleaner multi-tenant story, but adds a second entity type and a join the generic store does not express.
candidate_solutions.global_single_domain: One custom domain for the whole deployment, a single record in a 'settings' collection. Simplest to build and adequate for a self-hosted open-source deployment, but wrong as soon as one operator serves several customers, and it makes per-customer branding impossible.

context.sourced: Qwilr: custom domain is set in 'Account Settings -> Custom Domain' and all pages of the account move host together.
context.hard_constraint: AGENTS.md: 'The only fixed vocabulary is the envelope: id, collection, room_id, revision, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at. Do not add a migration or a typed column to store a team's field.' So the domain must be a field inside records.data, not a new column.
context.capability_available: find() / ?where= resolves dotted JSON paths through the dynamic index, so grouping rooms by a shared domain value is possible with no schema change.
context.decided_already: Jev selected secret_is_identity (p=0.99): the link secret is the room's identity, the host is presentation.
